correctness.rationale: For the upper bound, the distinct special lines belonging to graph edges form a connected line-intersection system covering every configuration point. The first line uses at least three points; any later line sharing at least two old points lies in the old affine span, while a line sharing exactly one old point can add at most one dimension and must contribute at least two new points. Thus an affine dimension of \(d\) requires at least \(3+2(d-1)\) points. For trees, the diametral-path induction always removes either a pendant two-vertex path or two sibling leaves, and the two vertices can be restored on a new line through the attachment vertex outside the old span, adding exactly one dimension. Base cases \(n=3,4\) are collinear. The finite checker confirms the reduction on all 985 nonisomorphic trees through order 12; the infinite theorem rests on the proof, not on enumeration.

value.rationale: The result closes the exact value on the entire natural class of trees for a newly introduced graph dimension and simultaneously supplies a sharp universal upper bound for every connected graph. The line-intersection charging lemma explains structurally why one extra affine dimension costs at least two additional vertices after the first special line. This is not a parameter substitution or finite table: it converts a published one-sided forest bound into a complete infinite-class theorem and gives a reusable obstruction for arbitrary connected graphs.
